name: Login & Registration Forms with Validation
description: Sign-in, registration, and password reset forms that follow NIST SP 800-63B-4 for passwords, never reveal whether an email has an account, work with password managers and passkeys, and keep passwords out of URLs, spell-check services, and plain view, with field errors and busy states that keep focus where people are.

tokens.note: Suggested defaults. The project's design tokens and existing forms win.

aiAgentInstructions.summary: Build or fix sign-in, registration, and password reset forms. Password rules, rate limits, and passkey support come from the project's authentication service when it has one; otherwise use this guide's NIST SP 800-63B-4 defaults. Public messages always follow this guide's account-privacy rules: map the service's error codes to them. Forms post, passwords stay out of spell-check services and plain view, password managers and paste always work, and busy states keep focus. Build on the project's form, field, and button components, and its validation (the Form Validation Pattern). Implement only what the task needs, keep existing APIs, and match the project's styling and tokens. The project's conventions win for styling and visual defaults; if one conflicts with an accessibility or correctness requirement in this guide, ask the user instead of choosing silently. Target WCAG 2.2 AA.
keyFeatures: Sign-in checks only that a password is there, so accounts made under older rules still work
Registration and reset follow NIST SP 800-63B-4: length, common and breached passwords, and no composition rules
Messages never reveal whether an email has an account: one sign-in failure message, the same next step after every registration, and the same confirmation after every reset request
A network or service failure gets its own message, so an outage never sends people to reset their password
Forms post (method="post"), so a password never ends up in a URL
A Show password toggle with aria-pressed that keeps focus; the password is hidden again when the form is sent or reset, or the page comes back
spellcheck="false" on password fields, the right autocomplete values, and paste always allowed (WCAG 2.2 3.3.8)
A busy Sign in button with aria-disabled that keeps focus and ignores a second press
Optional passkey sign-in with a fallback to the password form
implementationSteps: 1. Detect the framework and its version, the styling system, the tokens, and the existing components (projectDetection), plus the project's form library and validation.

2. Find how the project handles authentication: its own backend, or a provider or library, such as Auth0, Clerk, Supabase Auth, Firebase Auth, Amazon Cognito, or Auth.js. If it defines password rules, rate limits, or passkey support, follow them and use its components or SDK; this guide fills the gaps and doesn't override them. Map its error codes to implementationDetails.messages, and never show messages that reveal whether an account exists. If the service can't avoid revealing that, tell the user about the conflict instead of shipping it.
3. Choose the forms the task needs: sign-in, registration, password reset request (featureSpec.screens). Leave out the rest.
4. Build each form as in frameworkPatterns.signInForm: method="post", a heading that names it, a status region, and the fields with their autocomplete values.

5. Add the Show password toggle (frameworkPatterns.passwordToggle) and, for registration and reset, the requirements indicator (frameworkPatterns.passwordRequirements, implementationDetails.passwordRules).
6. Apply the Form Validation Pattern's timing to the fields, and send the form as in frameworkPatterns.signInSubmit.
7. Add passkeys or social sign-in only if the task asks for them (implementationDetails.passkeys).
8. Check the result against testingChecklist with a keyboard, a screen reader, a password manager, and a phone, and run the project's existing tests and checks.

featureSpec.goal: Let people create an account, sign in, and ask for a password reset with their password manager, keyboard, or screen reader, without revealing who has an account and without leaking passwords.
userJourney: Someone opens the sign-in page; the form is named by its heading "Sign in"
They enter their email and password, typed, pasted, or filled by a password manager
They press Sign in; the button stays focused with aria-disabled, and the status region says "Signing in…"
On success, they go on to the app
On wrong details, the status region says "Email or password is incorrect", the email stays, and the button works again
On a network or service failure, it says "Unable to sign in right now. Try again shortly" instead
From the sign-in page they can go to registration, where every valid submission leads to the same "Check your email to continue" step
From the sign-in page they can ask for a password reset, which always confirms the same way

screens.purpose: Sign in with an email and a password, or a passkey.

validation.email: Required, a valid email address, checked with the Form Validation Pattern's timing.
validation.password: Required: checked for presence only. No length or character rules at sign-in, so accounts made under older rules still work.

interactions.accessibilityNotes: Field errors first, as in the Form Validation Pattern. Focus stays where it was, on the button or in the field where Enter was pressed (frameworkPatterns.signInSubmit).

interactions.when: the browser and the auth service support passkeys
interactions.accessibilityNotes: If the prompt is cancelled or fails, focus returns to the passkey button, a short generic message shows in the status region, and the password form stays available.

ui.heading: Create an account
fields: password (autocomplete="new-password", spellcheck="false") with the requirements indicator
extras: terms checkbox, if the product needs one
ui.switchPrompt: Already have an account? Sign in

validation.name: Required, with no minimum length: some names are one character.
validation.email: Required and a valid email address. No availability check and no "already registered" error: both reveal which emails have accounts.
validation.passwordConfirmation: Must match, with the Form Validation Pattern's timing: checked when left, then on every input once it shows "Passwords must match".

screens.purpose: Ask for a password reset link.

validation.email: Required and a valid email address.

edgeCases: An email that already has an account: registration shows the same next step as for a new email, and the backend emails the account's owner a sign-in or reset link instead
An older account whose password is shorter than today's minimum still signs in; ask for a new password after sign-in only if the auth service requires it
A password filled by a password manager or pasted is accepted
Spaces and Unicode in a password are kept as typed, never trimmed
Too many attempts: the generic rate-limit message, worded the same whether or not the account exists
A passkey prompt cancelled or failed: the password form stays, and focus returns to the passkey button
A request that never answers ends at the time limit with the network message, and pressing Sign in again retries
A product that signs new users in immediately can't hide at registration whether an email has an account: raise that tradeoff with the user
Long emails and names scroll inside their fields, and nothing is cut off

dataContract.signInRequest: POST with email and password as typed; never in the URL.
dataContract.registrationRequest: POST with name, email, and password; the answer looks the same for new and existing emails (the account is created, or its owner is emailed).
dataContract.answers: Map the auth service's answers to implementationDetails.messages: wrong details, rate limits, and failures each have one public message, the same for every account.

requirements.1.3.1: Each form is named by its heading, and every field has a visible label.
requirements.1.3.5: Fields have autocomplete values: username, current-password, new-password, name, and one-time-code.
requirements.2.4.3: A failed submit moves focus to the first invalid field; switching forms moves it to the new form's heading.
requirements.2.5.8: Buttons, including Show password, are at least 24 by 24 px.
requirements.3.3.1: Field errors are shown in text next to their fields.
requirements.3.3.2: Required and optional fields say so in words.
requirements.3.3.3: Field errors say how to fix them, except where they must stay generic.
requirements.3.3.8: No cognitive test without an alternative: paste and password managers always work, and passkeys or email links are offered where the auth service supports them.
requirements.4.1.2: The Show password toggle exposes its state with aria-pressed.
requirements.4.1.3: "Signing in…", sign-in results, and the requirement status are announced through one status region per form.

keyboardNavigation.enter: Enter in any field sends the form.
keyboardNavigation.showPassword: Space or Enter toggles it, and focus stays on it.
keyboardNavigation.order: Fields, Show password, Sign in, then the links.

form.aria-labelledby: The form's heading, so it is named, without role="form"

showPassword.aria-pressed: "true" while the password is shown; the name stays "Show password"

screenReader.formName: The heading names the form, and the page title says which form it is.
screenReader.status: "Signing in…", the sign-in results, and the requirement status, each once, through the form's status region.
screenReader.fieldErrors: As in the Form Validation Pattern: read with their fields, never live regions.

formSwitch.effect: A fade between sign-in and registration

animations.reducedMotion: Under prefers-reduced-motion: reduce, changes are instant.

framework.description: Find the framework, its version, and how existing components are written before writing code.
detectionSteps: Read the project's dependencies (package.json or its equivalent) for the framework and its version, and use the syntax that version supports.
Open two or three existing components to see their file structure, state handling, and naming.
Look for an existing component that already does this job, in the project or in a design system or UI library it uses, and build on it.

stylingSystem.description: Use the styling system the project already uses, and only that one.
detectionSteps: Check the dependencies and config for the styling setup: Tailwind (version 4 keeps its theme in CSS with @theme, version 3 in tailwind.config.*), CSS Modules, Sass, CSS-in-JS, or plain CSS.
See how existing components apply styles and compose class names, for example with cn or clsx.
Check for design documentation: DESIGN.md, a design system package, or Storybook stories for existing components.
adaptationRules: Write styles the way existing components do, and add no new styling library or system.
With plain CSS, use classes in the project's stylesheets instead of inline styles, except for values computed at runtime.
If the setup is unclear or mixed, ask before choosing.

designTokens.description: Use the project's tokens for color, spacing, radius, type, shadows, motion, and layering.
detectionSteps: Find the tokens: CSS custom properties, a Tailwind theme (@theme or config), a theme object, or a tokens file.
Use them instead of this guide's example values; where there are none, match the closest existing components.
Check that the colors you use meet the contrast minimums: 4.5:1 for text, and 3:1 for focus indicators, icons, and control boundaries.

frameworkPatterns.note: Short snippets in plain HTML and JavaScript for the parts that are easiest to get wrong; adapt them to the project's framework and its version.

signInForm.description: The sign-in form: method="post", named by its heading, a status region, autocomplete values, spellcheck="false" on the password, and the Show password toggle's markup.
signInForm.html:
Sign in

Forgot your password?

passwordToggle.description: The Show password toggle: a stable name with aria-pressed, focus kept, and the password hidden again when the form is sent or reset, or the page comes back from the back/forward cache.

signInSubmit.description: Sending the sign-in: a busy button with aria-disabled that keeps focus, a second press ignored, a time limit, and separate messages for wrong details, rate limits, and failures.

passwordRequirements.description: The requirements indicator's state for registration and reset: too short, too common, or meets the requirements, counted in Unicode code points.

implementationDetails.passwordRules: Take the rules from the auth service when it has them. Otherwise, NIST SP 800-63B-4: at least 15 characters when the password is the only sign-in factor, and at least 8 when a second factor is always required; accept at least 64 characters, spaces, all printable characters, and Unicode, and don't trim or truncate them; no composition rules, so never ask for digits, symbols, or mixed case; and reject common and breached passwords, with the full check on the server. Count length in Unicode code points. Sign-in checks presence only.
implementationDetails.requirementsIndicator: For registration and reset: too short, too common, or meets the requirements (frameworkPatterns.passwordRequirements). It never says "strong" from length or character types; a pattern-aware strength estimator the project already has may rate instead. Its status is announced when it changes, through the form's status region, not on every keystroke.

messages.serviceUnavailable: Unable to sign in right now. Try again shortly
messages.resetRequested: If an account exists for this email, we've sent a reset link
messages.rateLimited: Too many attempts. Wait a few minutes and try again
messages.fieldMessages: Field errors stay specific: "Enter your email address", "Use at least 15 characters", "This password is too common. Choose a different one", "This password has appeared in a data breach. Choose a different one", and "Passwords must match".
messages.placement: Sign-in results show at the top of the form, in its status region, with the email kept.

implementationDetails.accountPrivacy: Never reveal whether an email has an account: one sign-in failure message; the same next step after every valid registration, while the backend emails the existing account's owner instead; the same confirmation after every reset request; and rate-limit messages worded the same for every account. Registration needs email verification for this; if the product signs new users in immediately, raise the tradeoff with the user.
implementationDetails.passwordsInTheBrowser: Forms post (method="post"): a form sent before its script runs, on a slow connection or a server-rendered page before hydration, would otherwise use GET and put the email and password in the URL, where history and server logs keep them. Password fields have spellcheck="false" and autocapitalize="none": shown as text, a password could otherwise reach a browser's online spell-check service (Chrome's Enhanced Spell Check and Microsoft Editor, when turned on; reported in 2022). The password is hidden again when the form is sent or reset, and when the page comes back from the back/forward cache (frameworkPatterns.passwordToggle).
implementationDetails.passwordManagers: autocomplete="username" on the email that identifies the account, also when it holds an email address; current-password at sign-in; new-password at registration and reset; one-time-code on verification codes. Never block paste or autofill (WCAG 2.2 3.3.8).
implementationDetails.sending: Validation runs first, with the Form Validation Pattern's timing. While the request runs, the button has aria-disabled="true", ignores another press, and keeps focus; the status region says "Signing in…". Don't disable the fields or the button: disabling the focused element drops focus to the page in Chromium and Firefox (checked). The request has a time limit (30 seconds, suggested); a timeout or a dropped connection gets the network message, never the wrong-details one.
implementationDetails.passkeys: Optional: a "Sign in with a passkey" button, and passkey autofill with autocomplete="username webauthn" on the email field. If the prompt is cancelled or fails, focus returns to the passkey button, a short generic message shows, and the password form stays.
implementationDetails.showPassword: A <button type="button"> next to the field, named "Show password", with aria-pressed; its name stays the same, screen readers announce its state, and focus stays on it. A "Show password" checkbox works too.

must: Follow the auth service's password rules, rate limits, and passkey support when it has them, and map its errors to this guide's public messages
Post the forms, and keep passwords out of URLs
Keep sign-in to a presence check, and registration and reset to the NIST rules
Keep messages generic wherever they could reveal whether an account exists
Use the project's framework version, styling system, and tokens, the way existing components do
mustNot: Add an auth, form, or password-strength library without asking
Ask for digits, symbols, or mixed case, or say "strong" from length alone
Say "user not found", "email already in use", or which field was wrong at sign-in
Block paste or autofill, or leave spell check on password fields
Disable the focused button or the fields while signing in
Use inline styles for static values in a plain-CSS project, or hardcode colors the project has tokens for

testingChecklist: Each form posts (method="post"), so a form sent before its script runs never puts a password in the URL
Sign-in accepts any non-empty password; registration and reset apply the length, common-password, and breach rules, with no composition rules
Passwords of 64 or more characters, spaces, and Unicode are accepted as typed
The requirements indicator never says "strong" from length alone, and screen readers hear its status when it changes
A failed sign-in says "Email or password is incorrect", a network or service failure says "Unable to sign in right now", and the email stays filled in
Registration, password reset, and rate-limit messages read the same whether or not the account exists
Password managers can save and fill the credentials, and paste works in every field
Show password keeps its name and focus, shows its state with aria-pressed, and the password is hidden again when the form is sent or reset, or the page comes back
While signing in, the button keeps focus with aria-disabled, a second press sends nothing, and the status region says "Signing in…"
Field errors follow the Form Validation Pattern, and a failed submit moves focus to the first invalid field
Passkey sign-in, if offered, falls back to the password form when it's cancelled or fails
The forms work at 320 px wide, with 16 px text on phones
Styles come from the project's styling system and tokens
